title: Plus (+) Star Pattern
description: Brute force to optimized: dual row-or-column per-cell checks versus classifying each row once and building it directly, then batching the whole pattern into one output call.

blocks.text: Given a positive odd integer n, print an n by n grid where a star appears anywhere on the single middle row or the single middle column, with a space everywhere else, forming a plus shape.

blocks.title: Analogy: Two Strips of Tape Forming a Plus Sign
blocks.text: Picture two straight strips of tape laid across a square sheet of paper, one running horizontally through the exact middle row, and the other running vertically through the exact middle column. Together, right where they overlap, they form a plus sign, while the four corner regions of the sheet stay completely bare.

blocks.caption: The middle row and the middle column together form a plus shape

blocks.content: {"headers":["Row","Output","Why"],"rows":[["Row 1","  *  ","A side row, not the middle row, so only column mid, which is 2, gets a star."],["Row 2","  *  ","Still a side row, the same single star at column mid."],["Row 3","*****","This is row mid, the middle row, so the entire row is solid stars."],["Row 4","  *  ","Back to a side row, the single star at column mid again."],["Row 5","  *  ","The final side row, matching every other side row exactly."]]}

blocks.text: A single cell, which is both the middle row and the middle column at once, so it is simply a single star.
This shape looks new, but it is worth checking how much of it is already covered by two ideas already used earlier in this division.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Just like the hollow square, testing a small example shows this shape has only two distinct row types, the single middle row, which is entirely solid stars, and every other row, which is otherwise identical to every other side row.

Observation 2: Unlike the hollow square's middle rows, which had two stars at fixed edge columns, here every side row has exactly one star, and it always sits at the same known column, mid, regardless of which side row it is.

Observation 3: That single, isolated star at a known column index is exactly the direct-index-placement idea already used for the cross pattern's two diagonal stars, just applied here to only one star instead of two.

Observation 4: So this shape needs no new technique at all, it is the hollow square's two-row-type classification combined with the cross pattern's direct single-index placement, applied to whichever row type a given row belongs to.
Naming both of those reused ideas explicitly, row classification and direct index placement, turns this from an unfamiliar shape into a straightforward combination of two techniques already in hand.
Use two nested loops covering every row and column, and for each individual cell, check whether its row is the middle row or its column is the middle column.

items: Compute mid, the index of the single middle row and column.
Loop over each row i and each column j inside it.
For every cell, check if i equals mid, or j equals mid.
If either is true, print a star.
Otherwise print a space.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: check both the middle row and middle column conditions for every cell

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: mid is computed once for the whole grid, since the middle row and column index never changes across any row or column.
Both conditions, i equals mid and j equals mid, are checked together for every one of the n squared cells, even though for most rows only one column, mid, will ever be a star.
A single character, star or space, is printed per innermost iteration, keeping the per cell cost of this version fully visible.

blocks.text: This is correct, since every cell is individually tested against both the middle row and middle column conditions before deciding what to print.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), since every one of the n squared cells requires its own two part condition check.
Space: O(1) extra space, no string is ever built.

Limitation: checking both conditions for every single cell is wasteful, since a row is either entirely the middle row, every cell a star, or it is one of the other rows, with exactly one star at the middle column. That classification only needs to happen once per row, not once per cell.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking every column works but is wasteful: the row-level fact, is this the middle row, and the single known star column, mid, both get re-derived once per column instead of once per row.

What stays the same as two earlier problems in this division: the two-row-type classification from the hollow square, and the direct single-index star placement from the cross pattern.

What is different here: the middle row is solid, exactly like the hollow square's border rows, but every side row has only a single, isolated star, placed directly at mid, exactly like one of the cross pattern's two diagonal placements.

Can both reused techniques apply unchanged: yes, classify the row once, then either build it as a solid run, or start it blank and place one star directly at mid.

The core idea: classify each row as the middle row or a side row, then build the middle row as a solid run of stars, or a side row as a blank row with a single star placed directly at column mid.

Classify each row just once: the middle row is entirely stars, while every other row is blank except for a single star at the middle column. Build that row directly with one operation, replacing n individual cell checks with a single row level decision.
For each row, decide once whether it is the middle row or a side row, then build that row directly and print it once.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: decide the row type once, then build it directly

blocks.text: This works because a row's entire shape depends only on whether its row index equals mid, a single per row decision, and once that classification is made, the row content is fully determined; a direct repeat operation constructs the solid middle row in one step, and a blank row with a single star placed directly at index mid constructs every side row just as directly, with no dependence on checking individual columns.

items: mid is computed once for the entire grid, since it never changes across rows or columns.
The middle row is built with a single repeat operation producing n stars, exactly the same direct-construction technique used for solid rows throughout this division.

Every side row is built by starting from a blank row of n spaces and placing a single star directly at index mid, the exact same direct-index-placement technique already used for the cross pattern's diagonal stars.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) total characters produced, the same as the brute force, but with only one row level decision per row instead of n per cell checks, and O(n) print calls instead of O(n squared).
Space: O(n), for the single row string being built and printed at a time.
10. Further Optimization: A Single Output Call

Since there are only ever two distinct row shapes, the solid middle row and the single star side row, both can be built once, reused for every matching row, joined together with newline characters, and the entire pattern can be produced with a single output call.

blocks.caption: Further optimization: reuse the two row shapes and output the whole pattern in one call

codes.python:
def plus_pattern(n):
    mid = n // 2
    full_row = "*" * n                          # the middle row is identical to itself only once
    side_row = " " * mid + "*" + " " * (n - mid - 1)  # every other row is identical to each other
    rows = [full_row if i == mid else side_row for i in range(n)]
    print("\n".join(rows))                       # join every row and output the whole pattern at once


if __name__ == "__main__":
    plus_pattern(5)

items: The solid middle row shape and the single-star side row shape are each built exactly once, before any row assembly begins, since reusing them is possible precisely because only two distinct shapes ever occur.
Every row in the final list simply selects one of those two already-built shapes according to its classification, with no repeated construction work per row.
Joining all n selected rows with newline characters and printing once collapses the output down to a single call, regardless of how large n is.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), the same total characters produced.
Space: O(n squared), to hold every row joined into one string before the single output call. This trades some memory for the fewest possible output calls, exactly one, no matter how large n is.

blocks.text: Like the hollow square solved earlier, this shape has only two distinct row forms, and recognizing that up front turns a dense grid of per cell checks into a handful of direct row level operations. Any pattern built from full rows and columns, rather than diagonals, tends to reduce to this same small number of row shapes.

items: Using integer division incorrectly for the middle index on an even n, this pattern is normally only defined for odd n, where a single middle row and column both exist.
Forgetting that the middle row itself is entirely stars, not a single star like every other row.
Off by one errors in the side row, the single star should land exactly at column mid, not mid plus or minus one.

blocks.text: Stating up front that this shape reduces to exactly two row types, just like the earlier hollow square, is a strong signal of pattern recognition, and it is worth explicitly asking whether n is guaranteed to be odd before writing any code.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "how many row types does this shape have", think: exactly two, just like the hollow square, name them explicitly before coding.
If the interviewer says "can you avoid checking every cell", think: classify the row once, then either build a solid run or place a single star directly at mid.
If the interviewer says "what if n is even", think: there is no single middle row or column, so clarify that assumption with the interviewer first.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: All three versions produce the same O(n squared) total characters, since that is fixed by the shape itself. What changes is how that output is organized: a two part per cell check in the brute force version, a single row-type decision per row in the optimized version, and exactly one call for the entire pattern in the further optimized version.

items: Pattern: grid pattern printing that combines two ideas already used in this division, classifying rows into a small number of types, and placing an isolated star at one directly known column index.

Core Idea: classify each row as the middle row or a side row, then build the middle row as a solid run of stars, or a side row as a blank row with a single star placed directly at column mid, reusing the hollow square's row classification and the cross pattern's direct placement.
Time: O(n squared) checks for the brute force, O(n) output calls for the optimized version, O(1) for the further optimized version; total characters printed are always O(n squared).
Space: O(1) extra for the brute force, O(n) for the current row, O(n squared) for the fully joined pattern.
Most Important Observation: an unfamiliar shape can often be assembled directly from two techniques already used on earlier problems, row classification and direct index placement.
Interview Difficulty: easy to produce the correct shape with two conditions per cell; explicitly naming both reused techniques is what shows real pattern recognition.
One line memory trick: two row types, like the hollow square; a single star at mid, like the cross pattern.
